findings.title: Denial cache key construction is ambiguous and can produce collisions
findings.body: userPermDenialCacheKey concatenates namespace, userUID, action, name, and parent using underscores as separators, but these components can themselves contain underscores. For example, userPermDenialCacheKey("org-1", "u1", "dashboards:read", "my_dash", "folder1") produces the same key as userPermDenialCacheKey("org-1", "u1", "dashboards:read", "my", "dash_folder1"). A denial cached for one resource would incorrectly deny access to a different resource. Consider using a separator that cannot appear in UIDs/names (e.g., a null byte or a structured encoding), or hashing the components individually.

findings.title: Denial cache can block access to a resource immediately after it is created
findings.body: The denial cache is checked first (line 117) and returns deny immediately if hit, without re-checking the database. If a user's request for a not-yet-existing resource is denied and that denial is cached (line 154), then the resource is created (granting the user permission), subsequent checks for up to shortCacheTTL (30 seconds) will still return deny from the stale denial cache entry. This partially undermines the PR's stated goal of letting creators access newly created dashboards/folders, particularly in UI flows that may pre-check permissions before creation completes.

findings.title: Every denied request that misses the denial cache triggers a full DB permission query
findings.body: When the permission cache is hit but does not contain the requested scope (i.e., the user has some permissions but not for this specific resource), the code falls through to getIdentityPermissions which queries the database. Previously the cached permission set was authoritative for both allow and deny. Now, every check for a resource not in the cached set hits the DB until the denial cache entry is written. In high-cardinality environments (many users checking many distinct resources they lack access to), this can significantly increase database load during the initial warm-up period before denial cache entries are populated.

findings.title: permissionCacheUsage metric incremented as 'false' even when permission cache was hit but simply didn't allow
findings.body: At line 137, s.metrics.permissionCacheUsage.WithLabelValues("false", ...) is incremented whenever the code falls through the cached-permission check, including the case where getCachedIdentityPermissions succeeded (err == nil) but checkPermission returned false. This conflates 'cache miss' with 'cache hit but denied', making it harder to distinguish actual cache effectiveness from the expected deny-after-hit path. The metric label 'false' suggests a cache miss, but it was actually a cache hit that simply didn't grant access.
